7221	## TimeCompletion (whole result)
  7222	
  7223	Covers two modules, `TimeCompletion` and `MaskedContinuousWaveCompleted`, on
  7224	`notes/integrated_covariance_foundation.tex` at `a284420`. It formalizes
  7225	`L:masked-time-completion` (lines 141-156, display `E:masked-time-schur` at
  7226	150-152, proof 158-181) with the completion `H_a` constructed. It re-issues
  7227	`L:masked-trig-products` (lines 347-374) and `L:masked-continuous-wave`
  7228	(lines 378-423, display `E:masked-continuous-wave` at 385-389) in this
  7229	concrete `H_a`, with nothing supplied. Standing hypotheses: `T > 0` and
  7230	`0 < a < 1` (the section's `a = alpha0`, lines 4-7). The section also assumes
  7231	`H:homog` and `Gamma != 0`, but lines 5-7 say the purely temporal estimates
  7232	hold independently of `Gamma`. These lemmas are purely temporal, so neither
  7233	hypothesis is assumed.
  7234	
  7235	What is constructed. `L2fun T` is complex `L^2(0,T)` as a space of
  7236	functions (`MemLp f 2 (volume.restrict (Icc 0 T))`). On it,
  7237	`TimeSchur.timeForm` (`<f,g>_a = int int f(t) conj g(s) |t-s|^(-a)`) is a
  7238	Hermitian sesquilinear form (`conj_timeForm`, `timeForm_add_right`,
  7239	`timeForm_smul_right`) and is positive semidefinite (`timeForm_re_nonneg`).
  7240	These are the axioms of a pre-inner product (`core`; the arguments are
  7241	swapped because Mathlib's inner product is conjugate-linear in the first
  7242	slot). `Ha p` is Mathlib's `UniformSpace.Completion` of the resulting
  7243	pre-Hilbert space `Pre p`, so it is a complex Hilbert space, and functions at
  7244	seminorm distance zero are identified (`coe_eq_of_ae`, the null quotient).
  7245	`emb p` is the inclusion of `L^2(0,T)`. Its squared norm is
  7246	`Re timeForm a T f f` (`emb_norm_sq`). This is faithful to the TeX's "null-quotient completion" for the following reason. The TeX completes the
  7247	real compact smooth tests and then complexifies. `dense_span_realTestSet`
  7248	proves that the complex span of the images of the real tests supported in
  7249	`(0,T)` is dense in `Ha p`. So `Ha p` is the closure of the complexified
  7250	tests, and its norm on a test is the TeX's form. `H_a` is built directly over
  7251	`C`. The TeX's real space is represented by the real functions of
  7252	`emb_norm_sq_real` and the positivity clause, not by a separate real
  7253	Hilbert space.
  7254	
  7255	The paper wrapper `masked_time_completion_paper` has exactly the hypotheses
  7256	`0 < a < 1`, `T > 0` and states, in eight conjuncts:
  7257	- positivity on real compact smooth tests, with integrability of the
  7258	  integrand;
  7259	- separability of `Ha p`;
  7260	- `E:masked-time-schur` for `||emb f||`;
  7261	- the continuous linear extension `extL2 p` on a.e.-classes of

  7264	  integral with `f(t) conj f(s)`, it is the sum of the squared norms of the

   199	 2072| \begin{lemma}[Two static contraction bounds]\label{L:phase-contractions}
   200	 2073|   For $\lambda > 0$, $q \in \R^3$, $a > 0$, and $\epsilon > 0$,
   201	 2074|   \begin{align}
   202	 2075|     \int_{\R^3}\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{\lambda^2+|q+\xi|^2}
   203	 2076|     &\le R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2},
   204	 2077|     \label{E:phase-resolvent}\\
   205	 2078|     \left|T_\epsilon(a,q)\right|
   206	 2079|     &\le D_\Gamma a^{1-\alpha},
   207	 2080|     \label{E:phase-trace}\\
   208	 2081|     T_\epsilon(a,q)
   209	 2082|     &:=\int_{\R^3}e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)
   210	 2083|     =\int_{\R^3}\widehat{G}_a(q+\xi)e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2}
   211	 2084|     \mu(\ud\xi).\nonumber
   212	 2085|   \end{align}
   213	 2086| \end{lemma}
   214	 2087| 
   215	 2088| \begin{proof}
   216	 2089|   Homogeneity and Fourier uniqueness give $\mu(B_r) = Vr^\alpha$. In particular,
   217	 2090|   there is no origin atom. For $s > 0$, Schwartz Fourier pairing yields
   218	 2091|   \[
   219	 2092|     \int e^{-s|q+\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
   220	 2093|     =\int p_{2s}(x)e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x)

221	 2094|     \le\int p_{2s}(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
   222	 2095|     =\int e^{-s|\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi).
   223	 2096|   \]
   224	 2097|   The integrals are finite. Evenness makes the middle integral real, and
   225	 2098|   nonnegativity of $\Gamma$ gives the inequality. Multiply by $e^{-\lambda^2s}$
   226	 2099|   and integrate in $s$. Nonnegative Tonelli on the spectral side gives the
   227	 2100|   resolvent comparison. At $q = 0$ its value is
   228	 2101|   \[
   229	 2102|     \alpha V\int_0^\infty\frac{r^{\alpha-1}}{\lambda^2+r^2}\ud r
   230	 2103|     =R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2}.
   231	 2104|   \]
   232	 2105|   This proves~\eqref{E:phase-resolvent}.
   233	 2106| 
   234	 2107|   Since $\mu$ is tempered, its Gaussian weighting is finite. Fourier Fubini
   235	 2108|   therefore gives the identity for $T_\epsilon$. The measure
   236	 2109|   $\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)$ is finite and nonnegative, whence
   237	 2110|   $|T_\epsilon(a,q)| \le T_\epsilon(a,0)$. The radial distribution function of
   238	 2111|   $\Gamma$ is $\Gamma(B_r) = Mr^{3-\alpha}$. Thus, for every nonnegative radial
   239	 2112|   Schwartz function $F$,
   240	 2113|   \[
   241	 2114|     \int F(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
   242	 2115|     =(3-\alpha)M\int_0^\infty F(r)r^{2-\alpha}\ud r
   243	 2116|     =c_\Gamma\int_{\R^3}F(x)|x|^{-\alpha}\ud x.
   244	 2117|   \]
   245	 2118|   Apply this to $F = G_a*p_{2\epsilon}$, which is radial and Schwartz.
   246	 2119|   Nonnegative Fubini gives
   247	 2120|   \[
   248	 2121|     T_\epsilon(a,0)
   249	 2122|     =c_\Gamma[p_{2\epsilon}*(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})](0)
   250	 2123|     \le c_\Gamma\sup_z(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z).
   251	 2124|   \]
   252	 2125|   Write $r = |z|$. The spherical wave measure has mass $a$, and direct
   253	 2126|   integration over its normal coordinate gives, for $r > 0$,
   254	 2127|   \[
   255	 2128|     (G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z)
   256	 2129|     =\frac{(a+r)^{2-\alpha}-|a-r|^{2-\alpha}}
   257	 2130|     {2r(2-\alpha)}.
   258	 2131|   \]
   259	 2132|   For $r < a/2$, distances from $z$ to the sphere are at least $a/2$, giving the
   260	 2133|   bound $2^\alpha a^{1-\alpha}$. For $r > 2a$, they are at least $a$, giving
   261	 2134|   $a^{1-\alpha}$. On $a/2 \le r \le 2a$, the displayed formula is at most
   262	 2135|   $3^{2-\alpha}a^{1-\alpha}/(2-\alpha)$. These bounds also cover the endpoints
   263	 2136|   by continuity and give~\eqref{E:phase-trace}. This proves
   264	 2137|   Lemma~\ref{L:phase-contractions}.
   265	 2138| \end{proof}

   326	 2531| \begin{lemma}[Exact cutoffs for finite Gaussian words]\label{L:finite-word-cutoff}

   328	 2533|   Gaussian coordinates, grouped by color $i$, and let $\mathscr{X}$ be a complex
   329	 2534|   Hilbert space. On Gaussian polynomials with coefficients in $\mathscr{X}$ set
   330	 2535|   \[

   332	 2537|   \]

   334	 2539|   bounded operators acting only on $\mathscr{X}$. Fix a word $i_1,\ldots,i_n$,
   335	 2540|   and let $r_i$ be the number of its occurrences of color $i$. If $N_i \ge r_i$
   336	 2541|   and $P$ projects each color onto total Hermite degree at most $N_i$, then, for
   337	 2542|   every $v \in \mathscr{X}$,
   338	 2543|   \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-word-cutoff}
   339	 2544|     \begin{split}
   340	 2545|       &(I\otimes F_n)(PJ_{i_n}P)(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
   341	 2546|       (PJ_{i_1}P)(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v)\\
   342	 2547|       &\qquad=(I\otimes F_n)J_{i_n}(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
   343	 2548|       J_{i_1}(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v).
   344	 2549|     \end{split}
   345	 2550|   \end{equation}

   347	 2552|   whenever the displayed vector integrals exist.

   352	 2557|   $h_{\boldsymbol a}$ to $\sqrt{a_{ij}+1}\,h_{\boldsymbol a+e_{ij}}
   353	 2558|   +\sqrt{a_{ij}}\,h_{\boldsymbol a-e_{ij}}$; the second term is zero if $a_{ij}

   728	  141| \begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}

   733	  146|   \]

   735	  148|   completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   736	  149|   from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   737	  150|   \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}

   739	  152|   \end{equation}

   741	  154|   $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a

   755	  168|     e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.

   771	   47| \begin{lemma}[Two Hermitian trace bounds]\label{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}
   772	   48|   Let $B,Y$ be finite Hermitian matrices, $m \ge 2$ an integer, and $L = 2m-2$.
   773	   49|   For integers $0 \le q \le L$,
   774	   50|   \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-word}
   775	   51|     \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(BY^qBY^{L-q})
   776	   52|     \le \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L).
   777	   53|   \end{equation}
   778	   54|   If $D \ge 0$ is Hermitian, then
   779	   55|   \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-holder}
   780	   56|     \operatorname{Tr}(D|Y|^{2m-2})
   781	   57|     \le (\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}
   782	   58|     (\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m})^{(m-1)/m}.
   783	   59|   \end{equation}
   784	   60| \end{lemma}
   785	   61| 
   786	   62| \begin{proof}
   787	   63|   Diagonalize $Y$, with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, and write $b_{ij}$ for the
   788	   64|   entries of $B$ in that basis. Hermitian symmetry gives $b_{ji} =
   789	   65|   \overline{b_{ij}}$. The trace word is the real sum
   790	   66|   \[
   791	   67|     \sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2\lambda_j^q\lambda_i^{L-q}.
   792	   68|   \]
   793	   69|   Bound each product by its absolute value and use
   794	   70|   \eqref{E:gaussian-integer-power}. After interchanging $i,j$, the two resulting
   795	   71|   sums agree because $|b_{ij}| = |b_{ji}|$. Each equals
   796	   72|   $\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2|\lambda_i|^L = \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L)$. The two
   797	   73|   weights sum to one, proving \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-word}. No commutation of
   798	   74|   $B$ and $Y$ is used.
   799	   75| 
   800	   76|   In the same basis put $d_i = D_{ii} \ge 0$. If $\theta_j$ are the nonnegative
   801	   77|   eigenvalues of $D$, a unitary change of basis gives $d_i =
   802	   78|   \sum_j|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j$. Both row and column sums of $|U_{ij}|^2$ equal one.
   803	   79|   Finite convexity therefore yields
   804	   80|   \[
   805	   81|     \sum_i d_i^m \le \sum_{i,j}|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j^m
   806	   82|     = \operatorname{Tr}D^m.
   807	   83|   \]

   810	   86|   inequality with $s$ equal to the weighted mean. Now apply finite H\"older from

  1146	   37| \begin{lemma}[Exact potential and mass]\label{L:temporal-equilibrium}
  1147	   38|   For $0 < a < 1$ put $r = (1-a)/2$ and, for $0 < t < 1$,
  1148	   39|   \begin{equation}\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-density}
  1149	   40|     f_a(t)=\frac{[t(1-t)]^{-r}}{\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}.
  1150	   41|   \end{equation}
  1151	   42|   This positive function belongs to $L^1(0,1)\cap L^2(0,1)$, and
  1152	   43|   \begin{align}
  1153	   44|     \int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_a(t)\ud t&=1
  1154	   45|     &&\text{for every }s\in[0,1],\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}\\
  1155	   46|     M_a:=\int_0^1f_a(t)\ud t
  1156	   47|     &=\frac{\Gamma_E((1+a)/2)}
  1157	   48|     {\Gamma_E(1+a)\Gamma_E((1-a)/2)}>0.
  1158	   49|     \label{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}
  1159	   50|   \end{align}
  1160	   51| \end{lemma}
  1161	   52| 
  1162	   53| \begin{proof}
  1163	   54|   The positive binomial series $(1-z)^{-p} = \sum_{n\ge0}(p)_nz^n/n!$, $p > 0$,
  1164	   55|   $0 \le z < 1$, follows directly as follows. Its coefficient ratio gives
  1165	   56|   uniform convergence on compact subintervals, including for its derivative.
  1166	   57|   Termwise differentiation gives $(1-z)y' = py$, $y(0) = 1$; hence $(1-z)^py$ is
  1167	   58|   constant one. Here $(p)_0 = 1$, $(p)_n = p(p+1)\cdots(p+n-1)$. All terms used
  1168	   59|   below are nonnegative, so Tonelli applies.
  1169	   60| 
  1170	   61|   For $0 < s < 1$ split the integral of $|s-t|^{2r-1}[t(1-t)]^{-r}$ into left
  1171	   62|   and right parts. In the left part, $t = su$ gives
  1172	   63|   \begin{align*}
  1173	   64|     L(s)
  1174	   65|     &=s^r\int_0^1(1-u)^{2r-1}u^{-r}(1-su)^{-r}\ud u\\
  1175	   66|     &=\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)s^r
  1176	   67|     \sum_{n\ge0}
  1177	   68|     \frac{(r)_n(1-r)_ns^n}{(1+r)_n n!}.
  1178	   69|   \end{align*}
  1179	   70|   The Beta ratio follows from the Gamma recurrence. Since $(r)_n/(1+r)_n =
  1180	   71|   r/(r+n)$, expanding the incomplete Beta integral gives

1181	   72|   \[
  1182	   73|     L(s)=r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)B_s(r,r),\qquad
  1183	   74|     B_s(r,r)=\int_0^s u^{r-1}(1-u)^{r-1}\ud u.
  1184	   75|   \]
  1185	   76|   Reflection makes the right part $L(1-s)$, while symmetry gives
  1186	   77|   $B_s(r,r)+B_{1-s}(r,r) = \operatorname{Beta}(r,r)$. The full integral is
  1187	   78|   therefore $r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)\operatorname{Beta}(r,r) =
  1188	   79|   \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$. All integrals are finite because $-r > -1$ and
  1189	   80|   $2r-1 > -1$. At $s = 0$ the integral is directly $\operatorname{Beta}(r,1-r) =
  1190	   81|   \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$; $s = 1$ follows by reflection. This proves
  1191	   82|   \eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}, including the endpoints without a
  1192	   83|   limiting argument there.
  1193	   84| 
  1194	   85|   Integrability and square integrability follow from $-r > -1$ and $-2r = a-1 >
  1195	   86|   -1$. Finally,
  1196	   87|   \[
  1197	   88|     M_a=
  1198	   89|     \frac{\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,1-r)}
  1199	   90|     {\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}
  1200	   91|     =\frac{\Gamma_E(1-r)}{\Gamma_E(2-2r)\Gamma_E(r)},
  1201	   92|   \]
  1202	   93|   which is~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}. Its time mass has not been
  1203	   94|   renormalized. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium}.
  1204	   95| \end{proof}

  1217	   50|   \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-static-score}
  1218	   51|     S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}\ge
  1219	   52|     \lambda_z(1)-\frac{M_a}{2}B_\Gamma(z,z).

  1229	   62|   $c > 0$. Comparing identical unit tests makes $\lambda_z(c)^2$ Lipschitz with

  1266	  101| \begin{lemma}[Deterministic Fourier bound for the spatial energy]
  1267	  102|   \label{L:spatial-fourier-bound}
  1268	  103|   Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, allowing $\Gamma=0$, let
  1269	  104|   $g\in C_c^\infty(\R^d;\R)$ satisfy $\|g\|_2=1$ and put
  1270	  105|   $b=\|\nabla g\|_2^2$. Then $b>0$ and
  1271	  106|   \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-fourier-bound}
  1272	  107|     0\le A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)
  1273	  108|     \le 2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2},
  1274	  109|   \end{equation}
  1275	  110|   where $R_\alpha$ is defined in~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}.
  1276	  111| \end{lemma}
  1277	  112| 
  1278	  113| \begin{proof}
  1279	  114|   If $b=0$, smoothness makes $\nabla g=0$ everywhere. Thus, $g$ is constant,
  1280	  115|   and compact support forces $g=0$, contrary to $\|g\|_2=1$. Put $Q=g^2$ and
  1281	  116|   use the unnormalized Fourier transform
  1282	  117|   \[
  1283	  118|     \mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)=\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q(x)\ud x.
  1284	  119|   \]
  1285	  120|   In the unitary convention of Section~\ref{S:masked-covariance}, this is
  1286	  121|   $c_d^{-1}\widehat Q$, with $c_d=(2\pi)^{-d/2}$.
  1287	  122|   The autocorrelation
  1288	  123|   \[
  1289	  124|     c_Q(y)=\int_{\R^d}Q(x)Q(x-y)\ud x
  1290	  125|   \]
  1291	  126|   is smooth and compactly supported. Apply the distributional spectral
  1292	  127|   identity~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to this Schwartz function.
  1293	  128|   Its inner Fourier integral is $|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2$, since $Q$ is real.
  1294	  129|   Hence
  1295	  130|   \[
  1296	  131|     A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)=\int c_Q(y)\Gamma(\ud y)
  1297	  132|     =\int|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\mu(\ud\xi).
  1298	  133|   \]
  1299	  134|   Both integrals are finite: $c_Q$ is compactly supported and $\Gamma$ is
  1300	  135|   Radon, while $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|^2$ is Schwartz and $\mu$ is tempered.
  1301	  136|   No density of either measure is required.
  1302	  137| 
  1303	  138|   Since $\|Q\|_1=1$, we have $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|\le1$. Integration by parts
  1304	  139|   and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality give
  1305	  140|   \[
  1306	  141|     |\xi|\,|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|
  1307	  142|     \le\|\nabla Q\|_1
  1308	  143|     \le2\|g\|_2\|\nabla g\|_2=2\sqrt b.
  1309	  144|   \]
  1310	  145|   Splitting into $|\xi|^2\le4b$ and $|\xi|^2>4b$ therefore yields
  1311	  146|   \[
  1312	  147|     |\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\le\frac{8b}{4b+|\xi|^2}.
  1313	  148|   \]
  1314	  149|   The deterministic resolvent calculation in the proof of
  1315	  150|   Lemma~\ref{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}, together
  1316	  151|   with~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}, gives, for $q>0$,
  1317	  152|   \[
  1318	  153|     \mathcal{R}_\Gamma(q):=\int\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{q^2+|\xi|^2}
  1319	  154|     =q^{\alpha-2}R_\alpha<\infty.
  1320	  155|   \]
  1321	  156|   Consequently,
  1322	  157|   \[
  1323	  158|     A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)\le8b\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(2\sqrt b)
  1324	  159|     =2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2}.
  1325	  160|   \]
  1326	  161|   Nonnegativity follows from the spectral identity. If $\Gamma=0$, then
  1327	  162|   $\mu=0$ and both sides of~\eqref{E:spatial-fourier-bound} vanish. This proves
  1328	  163|   Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-fourier-bound}.
  1329	  164| \end{proof}

  2043	\section{A static phase estimate at first variance order}
  2044	\label{S:static-phase}
  2045	
  2046	A time-block argument would have to carry both position and velocity. We
  2047	establish a uniform estimate for the first variance coefficient with arbitrary
  2048	deterministic initial phase. The covariance may be any member of the original
  2049	three-dimensional class; no endpoint representation is assumed. The estimate
  2050	below is not an all-order propagator bound.
  2051	
  2052	
  2053	
  2054	Let $0 < \alpha < 2$, and let $\Gamma$ be a nonnegative, even, positive-definite
  2055	tempered Radon covariance on $\R^3$, satisfying $\Gamma(rA) =
  2056	r^{3-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$. Its spectral convention is $\Gamma = \int e^{i\xi\cdot
  2057	x}\mu(\ud\xi)$. Put
  2058	\begin{equation}\label{E:phase-constants}
  2059	  \begin{split}
  2060	    V&=\mu(B_1),\qquad M=\Gamma(B_1),\qquad
  2061	    R_\alpha=\frac{\alpha\pi V}{2\sin(\pi\alpha/2)},\\
  2062	    c_\Gamma&=\frac{(3-\alpha)M}{4\pi},\qquad
  2063	    b_\alpha=2^\alpha+\frac{3^{2-\alpha}}{2-\alpha},\qquad
  2064	    D_\Gamma=c_\Gamma b_\alpha.
  2065	  \end{split}
  2066	\end{equation}
  2067	Here $B_1$ is the open unit ball in the relevant variable. The physical mass $M$
  2068	and the spectral mass $V$ are not identified. Let $p_\epsilon$ be the Brownian
  2069	Gaussian density with covariance $\epsilon I$, and set $\Gamma_\epsilon =
  2070	p_{2\epsilon}*\Gamma$.
  2071	
  2072	\begin{lemma}[Two static contraction bounds]\label{L:phase-contractions}
  2073	  For $\lambda > 0$, $q \in \R^3$, $a > 0$, and $\epsilon > 0$,
  2074	  \begin{align}
  2075	    \int_{\R^3}\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{\lambda^2+|q+\xi|^2}
  2076	    &\le R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2},
  2077	    \label{E:phase-resolvent}\\
  2078	    \left|T_\epsilon(a,q)\right|
  2079	    &\le D_\Gamma a^{1-\alpha},
  2080	    \label{E:phase-trace}\\
  2081	    T_\epsilon(a,q)
  2082	    &:=\int_{\R^3}e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)
  2083	    =\int_{\R^3}\widehat{G}_a(q+\xi)e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2}
  2084	    \mu(\ud\xi).\nonumber
  2085	  \end{align}
  2086	\end{lemma}
  2087	
  2088	\begin{proof}
  2089	  Homogeneity and Fourier uniqueness give $\mu(B_r) = Vr^\alpha$. In particular,
  2090	  there is no origin atom. For $s > 0$, Schwartz Fourier pairing yields
  2091	  \[
  2092	    \int e^{-s|q+\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
  2093	    =\int p_{2s}(x)e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x)
  2094	    \le\int p_{2s}(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
  2095	    =\int e^{-s|\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi).
  2096	  \]
  2097	  The integrals are finite. Evenness makes the middle integral real, and
  2098	  nonnegativity of $\Gamma$ gives the inequality. Multiply by $e^{-\lambda^2s}$
  2099	  and integrate in $s$. Nonnegative Tonelli on the spectral side gives the
  2100	  resolvent comparison. At $q = 0$ its value is
  2101	  \[
  2102	    \alpha V\int_0^\infty\frac{r^{\alpha-1}}{\lambda^2+r^2}\ud r
  2103	    =R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2}.
  2104	  \]
  2105	  This proves~\eqref{E:phase-resolvent}.
  2106	
  2107	  Since $\mu$ is tempered, its Gaussian weighting is finite. Fourier Fubini
  2108	  therefore gives the identity for $T_\epsilon$. The measure
  2109	  $\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)$ is finite and nonnegative, whence
  2110	  $|T_\epsilon(a,q)| \le T_\epsilon(a,0)$. The radial distribution function of
  2111	  $\Gamma$ is $\Gamma(B_r) = Mr^{3-\alpha}$. Thus, for every nonnegative radial
  2112	  Schwartz function $F$,
  2113	  \[
  2114	    \int F(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
  2115	    =(3-\alpha)M\int_0^\infty F(r)r^{2-\alpha}\ud r
  2116	    =c_\Gamma\int_{\R^3}F(x)|x|^{-\alpha}\ud x.
  2117	  \]
  2118	  Apply this to $F = G_a*p_{2\epsilon}$, which is radial and Schwartz.
  2119	  Nonnegative Fubini gives
  2120	  \[
  2121	    T_\epsilon(a,0)
  2122	    =c_\Gamma[p_{2\epsilon}*(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})](0)
  2123	    \le c_\Gamma\sup_z(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z).
  2124	  \]
  2125	  Write $r = |z|$. The spherical wave measure has mass $a$, and direct
  2126	  integration over its normal coordinate gives, for $r > 0$,
  2127	  \[
  2128	    (G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z)
  2129	    =\frac{(a+r)^{2-\alpha}-|a-r|^{2-\alpha}}
  2130	    {2r(2-\alpha)}.
  2131	  \]
  2132	  For $r < a/2$, distances from $z$ to the sphere are at least $a/2$, giving the
  2133	  bound $2^\alpha a^{1-\alpha}$. For $r > 2a$, they are at least $a$, giving
  2134	  $a^{1-\alpha}$. On $a/2 \le r \le 2a$, the displayed formula is at most
  2135	  $3^{2-\alpha}a^{1-\alpha}/(2-\alpha)$. These bounds also cover the endpoints
  2136	  by continuity and give~\eqref{E:phase-trace}. This proves

  2542	  every $v \in \mathscr{X}$,

  2546	      (PJ_{i_1}P)(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v)\\

  2559	  = 0$. Thus, it changes the total degree of color $i$ by one and leaves all

  7761	    -\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(\theta+\lambda)\big),\qquad\lambda>0.
  7762	  \end{equation}
  7763	  This is a positive integrable density, and
  7764	  \begin{equation}\label{E:clock-copy-obstruction}
  7765	    \begin{split}
  7766	      K_\Gamma(\theta)&=\int_0^\infty w_\theta(\lambda)\ud\lambda,\\
  7767	      0<J_{\Gamma,\rho}(\theta)
  7768	      &\le J_{\Gamma,1}(\theta)
  7769	      =\int_0^\infty
  7770	      \frac{2\theta}{2\theta+\lambda}w_\theta(\lambda)\ud\lambda
  7771	      <K_\Gamma(\theta).
  7772	    \end{split}
  7773	  \end{equation}
  7774	  When \(\alpha=1\),
  7775	  \begin{equation}\label{E:degree-one-clock-loss}
  7776	    J_{\Gamma,1}(\theta)=(2-2^a)K_\Gamma(\theta).
  7777	  \end{equation}
  7778	  Thus, this direct analytic clock-copying family, including independent clocks
  7779	  and a single shared clock, fails to reproduce the cross-pair transform
  7780	  throughout the original nonzero covariance class.
  7781	\end{proposition}
  7782	
  7783	\begin{proof}
  7784	  First evaluate the cross transform. Temporarily smooth the spatial covariance,
  7785	  so Fourier and time Fubini are absolute. For \(r=|\xi|\), direct integration
  7786	  over \(s=t+v\) and \(t=s+v\) gives
  7787	  \[
  7788	    \int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty
  7789	    e^{-\theta(s+t)-\lambda|s-t|}
  7790	    \widehat{G}_s(\xi)\overline{\widehat{G}_t(\xi)}\ud s\ud t
  7791	    =\frac{2\theta+\lambda}
  7792	    {2\theta(\theta^2+r^2)((\theta+\lambda)^2+r^2)} .
  7793	  \]
  7794	  For example, on the first cone the \(v\)-integral uses
  7795	  \[
  7796	    \int_0^\infty e^{-(\theta+\lambda)v}
  7797	    \sin(r(t+v))\ud v
  7798	    =\frac{(\theta+\lambda)\sin(rt)+r\cos(rt)}
  7799	    {(\theta+\lambda)^2+r^2}.
  7800	  \]
  7801	  Integrating the remaining sine-square and sine-cosine terms against
  7802	  \(e^{-2\theta t}\), and adding the second cone, gives the displayed identity.
  7803	  The value at \(r=0\) is its continuous limit.
  7804	
  7805	  The resulting spectral integrand is nonnegative. Removing the spatial Gaussian
  7806	  multiplier and using the Laplace formula for the power covariance therefore
  7807	  gives
  7808	  \[
  7809	    \begin{split}
  7810	      K_\Gamma(\theta)
  7811	      &=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)}
  7812	      \int_0^\infty\lambda^{a-1}
  7813	      \frac{2\theta+\lambda}{2\theta}
  7814	      \int\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}
  7815	      {(\theta^2+|\xi|^2)((\theta+\lambda)^2+|\xi|^2)}
  7816	      \ud\lambda\\
  7817	      &=\int_0^\infty w_\theta(\lambda)\ud\lambda.
  7818	    \end{split}
  7819	  \]
  7820	  The second equality is partial fractions, with
  7821	  \((\theta+\lambda)^2-\theta^2=\lambda(2\theta+\lambda)\). The smoothing
  7822	  passage is justified by monotone convergence in this nonnegative spectral
  7823	  expression and the finite quadratic form in
  7824	  Lemma~\ref{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}. Alternatively, homogeneity directly
  7825	  bounds the density near zero by a constant times \(\lambda^{a-1}\), and at
  7826	  infinity by a constant times \(\lambda^{a-2}\). Its strict positivity follows
  7827	  from \(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(\theta) -\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(\theta+\lambda)>0\),
  7828	  since \(\mu\ne0\).
  7829	
  7830	  The candidate integrals are well defined and positive. The bound
  7831	  \(\Psi_a(\theta|u-v|,v_\rho)\le (\theta|u-v|)^{-a}\), together with
  7832	  \(h_\Gamma(w)=h_\Gamma(1)w^{-\alpha/2}\), supplies an absolute majorant. With
  7833	  \(w=u+v\), \(q=u-v\), the Jacobian is \(1/2\) and \(-w<q<w\). It is a constant
  7834	  times
  7835	  \[
  7836	    \int_0^\infty e^{-\theta^2w/2}w^{-\alpha/2}
  7837	    \int_{-w}^w|q|^{-a}\ud q\ud w
  7838	    =\frac2{1-a}\int_0^\infty
  7839	    e^{-\theta^2w/2}w^{1-\alpha/2-a}\ud w<\infty .
  7840	  \]
  7841	  Here \(a<1\) and \(a+\alpha/2<2\). The same bound dominates the spatial
  7842	  heat-regularized averages, whose spatial factor is \(h_\Gamma(w+2\epsilon)\le
  7843	  h_\Gamma(w)\). This is an averaged spectral bound, not pointwise covariance
  7844	  monotonicity. Since \(v_\rho(u,v)\ge|u-v|=v_1(u,v)\), monotonicity of
  7845	  \(\Psi_a\) gives \(J_{\Gamma,\rho}\le J_{\Gamma,1}\).
  7846	
  7847	  We compute the latter by nonnegative Tonelli. Write
  7848	  \(A=\theta\lambda+\lambda^2/2\). Integration in \(q\) gives
  7849	  \(2(1-e^{-Aw})/A\). Also
  7850	  \[
  7851	    \mathcal{R}_\Gamma(q)
  7852	    =\frac12\int_0^\infty e^{-q^2w/2}h_\Gamma(w)\ud w,
  7853	  \]
  7854	  by the elementary resolvent integral and spectral Tonelli. Consequently,
  7855	  \[
  7856	    \begin{split}
  7857	      J_{\Gamma,1}(\theta)
  7858	      &=\frac1{4\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)}
  7859	      \int_0^\infty\frac{\lambda^{a-1}}A
  7860	      \int_0^\infty h_\Gamma(w)
  7861	      \left(e^{-\theta^2w/2}
  7862	      -e^{-(\theta+\lambda)^2w/2}\right)\ud w\ud\lambda\\
  7863	      &=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)}
  7864	      \int_0^\infty
  7865	      \frac{\lambda^{a-2}
  7866	      (\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(\theta)-\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(\theta+\lambda))}
  7867	      {2\theta+\lambda}\ud\lambda\\
  7868	      &=\int_0^\infty
  7869	      \frac{2\theta}{2\theta+\lambda}w_\theta(\lambda)\ud\lambda.
  7870	    \end{split}
  7871	  \]
  7872	  The \(q\)-integral's factor two cancels its coordinate Jacobian \(1/2\); the
  7873	  resolvent identity supplies the other factor two. Since \(w_\theta>0\) and
  7874	  \(2\theta/(2\theta+\lambda)<1\) for every \(\lambda>0\), the strict inequality
  7875	  follows.
  7876	
  7877	  Finally, if \(\alpha=1\), homogeneity gives
  7878	  \(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(q)=\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(1)/q\). Substitution in the two
  7879	  densities gives
  7880	  \[
  7881	    \begin{split}
  7882	      K_\Gamma(\theta)
  7883	      &=\frac{\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(1)}
  7884	      {2\theta^2\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)}
  7885	      \int_0^\infty\frac{\lambda^{a-1}}{\theta+\lambda}\ud\lambda,\\
  7886	      J_{\Gamma,1}(\theta)
  7887	      &=\frac{\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(1)}
  7888	      {\theta^2\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)}
  7889	      \int_0^\infty\lambda^{a-1}
  7890	      \left(\frac1{\theta+\lambda}
  7891	      -\frac1{2\theta+\lambda}\right)\ud\lambda .
  7892	    \end{split}
  7893	  \]
  7894	  The real Beta identity
  7895	  \[
  7896	    \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{a-1}}{x+c}\ud x
  7897	    =c^{a-1}\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(a)\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(1-a),
  7898	    \qquad c>0,
  7899	  \]
  7900	  follows by scaling and \((r,s)\mapsto(r+s,r/s)\) in the positive product of
  7901	  the two Gamma integrals. Their finiteness uses \(0<a<1\). Evaluation of these
  7902	  two integrals gives \(J_{\Gamma,1}/K_\Gamma=2(1-2^{a-1})=2-2^a\), proving
  7903	  \eqref{E:degree-one-clock-loss}. This proves
  7904	  Proposition~\ref{P:clock-copy-obstruction}.
  7905	\end{proof}
     1	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
     2	\label{S:masked-covariance}
     3	
     4	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
     5	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
     6	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
     7	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
     8	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
     9	\[
    10	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
    11	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
    12	\]
   141	\begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
   142	  Let $T > 0$. The form
   143	  \[
   144	    \langle f,g\rangle_a
   145	    = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
   146	  \]
   147	  is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
   148	  completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   149	  from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}
   151	    \|f\|_a^2 \le \frac{2T^{1-a}}{1-a}\|f\|_2^2.
   152	  \end{equation}
   153	  In its complexification the norm is given by the same double integral with
   154	  $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
   155	  subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.
   156	\end{lemma}
   157	
   158	\begin{proof}
   159	  Write $\Gamma_E$ for Euler's Gamma function. Away from the null diagonal,
   160	  \[
   161	    |t-s|^{-a} = \frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty
   162	    \lambda^{a-1}e^{-\lambda|t-s|}\ud\lambda.
   163	  \]
   164	  This follows by substitution in the defining Gamma integral. Moreover,
   165	  \[
   166	    e^{-\lambda|t-s|}
   167	    = \int_{-\infty}^{\min(t,s)}2\lambda
   168	    e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.
   169	  \]
   170	  For each $\lambda > 0$ its quadratic form is an integral of a square. All
   171	  exchanges for compact smooth tests are absolutely integrable because the
   172	  kernel row integral is at most $2T^{1-a}/(1-a)$. The same bound and $2|xy| \le
   173	  |x|^2+|y|^2$ prove~\eqref{E:masked-time-schur}. A countable $L^2$-dense family
   174	  of compact smooth tests is consequently dense in $H_a$, proving separability.
   175	  The complex quadratic form is the sum of those of the real and imaginary
   176	  parts, since symmetry cancels the imaginary cross term. Thus, the same bound
   177	  holds after complexification. Smooth density in $L^2$, together with the Schur
   178	  bound on the absolute bilinear form, extends the inclusion and the integral
   179	  identity to $L^2$. This includes the stated interval amplitudes. This proves
   180	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   181	\end{proof}
    47	\begin{lemma}[Two Hermitian trace bounds]\label{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}
    48	  Let $B,Y$ be finite Hermitian matrices, $m \ge 2$ an integer, and $L = 2m-2$.
    49	  For integers $0 \le q \le L$,
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-word}
    51	    \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(BY^qBY^{L-q})
    52	    \le \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L).
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	  If $D \ge 0$ is Hermitian, then
    55	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-holder}
    56	    \operatorname{Tr}(D|Y|^{2m-2})
    57	    \le (\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}
    58	    (\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m})^{(m-1)/m}.
    59	  \end{equation}
    60	\end{lemma}
    61	
    62	\begin{proof}
    63	  Diagonalize $Y$, with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, and write $b_{ij}$ for the
    64	  entries of $B$ in that basis. Hermitian symmetry gives $b_{ji} =
    65	  \overline{b_{ij}}$. The trace word is the real sum
    66	  \[
    67	    \sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2\lambda_j^q\lambda_i^{L-q}.
    68	  \]
    69	  Bound each product by its absolute value and use
    70	  \eqref{E:gaussian-integer-power}. After interchanging $i,j$, the two resulting
    71	  sums agree because $|b_{ij}| = |b_{ji}|$. Each equals
    72	  $\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2|\lambda_i|^L = \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L)$. The two
    73	  weights sum to one, proving \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-word}. No commutation of
    74	  $B$ and $Y$ is used.
    75	
    76	  In the same basis put $d_i = D_{ii} \ge 0$. If $\theta_j$ are the nonnegative
    77	  eigenvalues of $D$, a unitary change of basis gives $d_i =
    78	  \sum_j|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j$. Both row and column sums of $|U_{ij}|^2$ equal one.
    79	  Finite convexity therefore yields
    80	  \[
    81	    \sum_i d_i^m \le \sum_{i,j}|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j^m
    82	    = \operatorname{Tr}D^m.
    83	  \]
    84	  For completeness, the convexity step follows from $t^m \ge s^m+ms^{m-1}(t-s)$
    85	  for $s,t \ge 0$, obtained by differentiating the difference. Average this
    86	  inequality with $s$ equal to the weighted mean. Now apply finite H\"older from
    87	  Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers} to $\sum_i d_i|\lambda_i|^{2m-2}$. Since
    88	  $(2m-2)m/(m-1) = 2m$, the last display proves \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-holder},
    89	  including zero sums. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}.
    90	\end{proof}

1	\section{Compact mean families and the spectral gap for wave evolution}
     2	\label{S:compact-mean-family}
     3	
     4	Let $I = [0,1]$, let $K_x \subset \R^d$ be compact, and let $\sigma\mapsto
     5	V_\sigma$ be continuous from $I$ into $C_c^\infty(K_x)$, real and nonnegative.
     6	The index $\sigma$ is a family parameter, distinct from physical propagation
     7	time $t$. Assume that one real $w \in H^1(\R^d)$ with $\|w\|_2 = 1$ satisfies
     8	\begin{equation}\label{E:compact-common-trial}
     9	  \|\nabla w\|_2^2-\int V_\sigma w^2\le-\varepsilon
    10	  \quad\hbox{for all }\sigma\in I,\qquad \varepsilon>0.
    11	\end{equation}
    12	Put $M = \sup_I\|V_\sigma\|_\infty$ and $H_\sigma = -\Delta-V_\sigma$. The
    13	phases $E,F$, inclusion $i$, data $e_0$ and observable $O_\phi$ are exactly
    14	those of Section~\ref{S:constant-phase-young}.
    15	Proposition~\ref{P:constant-compact-base}, with deterministic coefficient $h =
    16	V_\sigma$ and noise amplitude zero, gives the ordinary physical flow
    17	$P_\sigma(t)$ on $F$. Its $E$ restriction is $P_\sigma^E(t)$. Uniqueness of the
    18	Duhamel solution makes finite-horizon constructions agree on overlaps; integer
    19	horizons and autonomy give the same semigroup for every $t \ge 0$.
    20	
    21	We import the following statements from the \emph{second edition}
    22	of~\cite{teschl:14:mathematical}: Theorem~10.2, p.~258, gives the self-adjoint
    23	$H^2$ operator, lower bound, essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$ and compact smooth
    24	core for real compact smooth potentials in the dimensions considered here.
    25	Theorem~10.13, p.~273, gives a simple positive ground state \emph{if the
    26	spectral bottom is an eigenvalue}. Theorem~4.12 and Corollary~4.13,
    27	pp.~140--141, give max--min and form monotonicity, with the essential threshold
    28	used after discrete eigenvalues end and with the quadratic-form domain allowed.
    29	Uniformity, fractional norms and all applications to $F$ are proved below.
    30	
    31	\subsection{The ground family and the global phase}
    32	
    33	\begin{proposition}[Ground states and a uniform rate gap]
    34	  \label{P:compact-ground-family}
    35	  The common form domain of $H_\sigma$ is $H^1$ with form $q_\sigma(u) =
    36	  \|\nabla u\|_2^2-\int V_\sigma|u|^2$. Its bottom $E_1(\sigma)$ is a simple
    37	  eigenvalue with a unique real positive-a.e. normalized ground state
    38	  $p_\sigma$. Let $E_2(\sigma)$ be the second max--min level, set to zero when
    39	  there is no second negative eigenvalue. Then
    40	  \begin{align}
    41	    -M&\le E_1(\sigma)\le-\varepsilon,\qquad
    42	    E_1(\sigma)<E_2(\sigma)\le0,\label{E:compact-energy-levels}\\
    43	    |E_j(\sigma)-E_j(\tau)|
    44	    &\le\|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_\infty,\qquad j=1,2.
    45	    \label{E:compact-level-continuity}
    46	  \end{align}
    47	  The map $\sigma\mapsto p_\sigma$ is continuous into $H^2$ and bounded there.
    48	  With $\lambda_\sigma = \sqrt{-E_1(\sigma)}$ and $\mu_\sigma =
    49	  \sqrt{-E_2(\sigma)}$,
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-rate-gap}
    51	    \sqrt\varepsilon\le\lambda_\sigma\le\sqrt M,\qquad
    52	    d_0:=\inf_I(\lambda_\sigma-\mu_\sigma)>0.
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{proposition}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  The imported Theorem~10.2 applies to $-V_\sigma$, which is real, compactly
    58	  supported and in $L^2$ for $d \le 3$. It gives the stated self-adjoint
    59	  operator on $H^2$ and essential threshold zero. Write $c = 1+M$ and $A_\sigma
    60	  = H_\sigma+c \ge 1$. On $H^2$, integration by parts and the spectral theorem
    61	  give
    62	  \[
    63	    \|A_\sigma^{1/2}u\|_2^2
    64	    =q_\sigma(u)+c\|u\|_2^2,\qquad
    65	    \|u\|_{H^1}^2\le\|A_\sigma^{1/2}u\|_2^2
    66	    \le c\|u\|_{H^1}^2.
    67	  \]
    68	  Spectral cutoffs $1_{[1,n]}(A_\sigma)u$ show that $H^2$ is a core for the
    69	  half-power form norm. Fourier cutoffs show it is dense in $H^1$. The two
    70	  equivalent completions are therefore $D(A_\sigma^{1/2})$ and $H^1$. Both norms
    71	  dominate $L^2$ and give the same $L^2$ limit, so these are equal as subspaces,
    72	  with the displayed form. This verifies the form domain used below.
    73	
    74	  The form lower bound and~\eqref{E:compact-common-trial} give $-M \le E_1 \le
    75	  -\varepsilon$ by the imported form max--min principle. The bottom belongs to
    76	  the spectrum and lies below the essential threshold, so it is an isolated
    77	  eigenvalue of finite multiplicity. Only now apply the imported Theorem~10.13:
    78	  it is simple with a positive ground state. Conjugation preserves the real
    79	  operator; positivity and unit $L^2$ norm fix its real representative.
    80	
    81	  Simplicity, isolation and threshold zero give $E_1 < E_2 \le 0$. For every
    82	  common unit form test, $|q_\sigma(u)-q_\tau(u)| \le
    83	  \|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_\infty$. Taking the same infima over orthogonal
    84	  complements and suprema in the source max--min formula proves
    85	  \eqref{E:compact-level-continuity}, including passage of $E_2$ to the
    86	  threshold. Compactness gives $\Delta_*: = \min_I(E_2-E_1) > 0$. Thus,
    87	  \[
    88	    \lambda_\sigma-\mu_\sigma
    89	    =\frac{E_2(\sigma)-E_1(\sigma)}
    90	    {\lambda_\sigma+\mu_\sigma}
    91	    \ge\frac{\Delta_*}{2\sqrt M}>0.
    92	  \]
    93	  Here $M \ge \varepsilon > 0$, and no division by $\mu_\sigma$ occurs.
    94	
    95	  Put $d_V = \|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_\infty$ and decompose $p_\tau = a p_\sigma+r$,
    96	  with $r\perp p_\sigma$ and $0 < a \le 1$. The variational bound gives
    97	  $q_\sigma(p_\tau) \le E_1(\sigma)+2d_V$, whereas the complementary spectral
    98	  bound gives $q_\sigma(p_\tau) \ge E_1(\sigma)+\Delta_*\|r\|_2^2$. Hence,
    99	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-ground-continuity}
   100	    \|p_\tau-p_\sigma\|_2^2
   101	    =2(1-a)\le2(1-a^2)\le4d_V/\Delta_*.
   102	  \end{equation}
   103	  The eigenfunction equation is
   104	  \[
   105	    (1-\Delta)p_\sigma
   106	    =(1-\lambda_\sigma^2+V_\sigma)p_\sigma.
   107	  \]
   108	  Its right side is continuous in $L^2$ and bounded there by $1+2M$. The inverse
   109	  of $1-\Delta$ is an isometry from $L^2$ to the Bessel $H^2$ space, proving the
   110	  asserted $H^2$ continuity and bound. This proves
   111	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-ground-family}.
   112	\end{proof}
   255	\begin{proposition}[The growing projection on the wave phase space]
   256	  \label{P:compact-F-projection}
   257	  The physical flow satisfies
   258	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-F-block}
   259	    P_\sigma(t)(e,c)
   260	    =\left(P_\sigma^E(t)e+
   261	    \int_0^tP_\sigma^E(t-r)D_\sigma C(r)c\ud r,\ C(t)c\right).
   262	  \end{equation}
   263	  Set
   264	  \begin{align}
   265	    f_\sigma&=\frac{\int V_\sigma p_\sigma}{2\lambda_\sigma}>0,
   266	    &\ell_\sigma^C(c)&=
   267	    f_\sigma\left(\frac{c_1}{\lambda_\sigma}
   268	    +\frac{c_2}{\lambda_\sigma^2}\right),
   269	    \label{E:compact-constant-dual}\\
   270	    e_\sigma&=ie_\sigma^E,
   271	    &\ell_\sigma(e,c)&=\ell_\sigma^E(e)+\ell_\sigma^C(c),\qquad
   272	    \Pi_\sigma=e_\sigma\ell_\sigma,\quad Q_\sigma=I-\Pi_\sigma.
   273	    \label{E:compact-F-projection}
   274	  \end{align}
   275	  These vectors, duals and rank-one projections are norm-continuous and
   276	  uniformly bounded, and
   277	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-F-eigen}
   278	    \ell_\sigma(e_\sigma)=1,\qquad
   279	    P_\sigma(t)\Pi_\sigma=\Pi_\sigma P_\sigma(t)
   280	    =e^{\lambda_\sigma t}\Pi_\sigma.
   281	  \end{equation}
   282	  For every fixed nonnegative smooth compact $\phi$ of integral one,
   283	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-positive-margins}
   284	    \inf_I\ell_\sigma(e_0)>0,\qquad
   285	    \inf_I O_\phi(e_\sigma)>0.
   286	  \end{equation}
   287	\end{proposition}
   288	
   289	\begin{proof}
   290	  The constant coordinates obey $C(t)$ because the potential force has range in
   291	  $iE$. To justify variation of constants on the $E$ component, let $g$ be a
   292	  continuous $E$ force and substitute the ordinary free-Duhamel equation for
   293	  $P_\sigma^E(t-r)g(r)$ in its time integral. With $B_\sigma^E(u,z) =
   294	  (0,V_\sigma u)$, strong $E$-valued Fubini gives
   295	  \begin{align*}
   296	    &\int_0^t\int_r^t S(t-s)B_\sigma^E
   297	    P_\sigma^E(s-r)g(r)\ud s\ud r\\
   298	    &\qquad=\int_0^tS(t-s)B_\sigma^E
   299	    \left[\int_0^sP_\sigma^E(s-r)g(r)\ud r\right]\ud s.
   300	  \end{align*}
   301	  All norms are bounded on the finite triangle, so this exchange is absolute in
   302	  $E$. Thus, $Y(t) = P_\sigma^E(t)e+\int_0^tP_\sigma^E(t-r)g(r)\ud r$ solves
   303	  free Duhamel with force $B_\sigma^EY+g$. Take $g(r) = D_\sigma C(r)c$ and
   304	  adjoin the constant block. This is the same $F$ Duhamel equation as the
   305	  ordinary flow; uniqueness proves~\eqref{E:compact-F-block}. Its finite-horizon
   306	  bounds are uniform since the family has bounded $L^\infty$ and $L^2$ norms on
   307	  one compact support.
   308	
   309	  The integral defining $f_\sigma$ is finite by $L^2$ Cauchy--Schwarz and
   310	  positive because $V_\sigma$ is nonzero by the common trial and $p_\sigma > 0$
   311	  a.e. Its coefficients are continuous and uniformly bounded by the $H^2$
   312	  continuity and positive lower bound for the rate; no $p_\sigma \in L^1$
   313	  assumption is used. Directly,
   314	  \begin{align*}
   315	    \ell_\sigma^ED_\sigma C(r)c&=f_\sigma(c_1+rc_2),\\
   316	    \ell_\sigma^C(c)
   317	    &=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda_\sigma r}
   318	    f_\sigma(c_1+rc_2)\ud r,\\
   319	    \ell_\sigma^C(C(t)c)
   320	    &=\int_t^\infty e^{\lambda_\sigma(t-r)}
   321	    f_\sigma(c_1+rc_2)\ud r.
   322	  \end{align*}
   323	  These integrals converge absolutely. Applying $\ell_\sigma$
   324	  to~\eqref{E:compact-F-block}, the finite integral and this tail combine to
   325	  give $\ell_\sigma P_\sigma(t) = e^{\lambda_\sigma t}\ell_\sigma$. The ground
   326	  mode also gives $P_\sigma(t)e_\sigma = e^{\lambda_\sigma t}e_\sigma$ and
   327	  $\ell_\sigma(e_\sigma) = 1$, proving~\eqref{E:compact-F-eigen}. Bounded
   328	  bilinear multiplication and the preceding continuous coefficients prove norm
   329	  continuity of all objects. Finally, $\ell_\sigma(e_0) =
   330	  f_\sigma/\lambda_\sigma > 0$ and $O_\phi(e_\sigma) = \int\phi p_\sigma > 0$.
   331	  Both are continuous on compact $I$, proving
   332	  \eqref{E:compact-positive-margins}. Positivity is in integrals, without a
   333	  point trace or a one-dimensional ODE. This proves
   334	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-F-projection}.
   335	\end{proof}
   336	
   337	\begin{proposition}[Complementary wave evolution and parameter dependence]
   338	  \label{P:compact-F-complement}
   339	  Uniformly over $\sigma$ and $t \ge 0$,
   340	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-F-complement}
   341	    \|P_\sigma(t)Q_\sigma\|_{\mathcal{B}(F)}
   342	    \le C(1+t)^3e^{\mu_\sigma t}.
   343	  \end{equation}
   344	  For every fixed $0 < \eta < d_0$,
   345	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-normalized-complement}
   346	    \|e^{-\lambda_\sigma t}P_\sigma(t)Q_\sigma\|
   347	    \le C_\eta e^{-\eta t}.
   348	  \end{equation}
   349	  For every finite $T_0$,
   350	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-parameter-flow}
   351	    \sup_{0\le t\le T_0}\|P_\sigma(t)-P_\tau(t)\|_{\mathcal{B}(F)}
   352	    \le C_{T_0}
   353	    \big(\|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_\infty+\|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_2\big).
   354	  \end{equation}
   355	\end{proposition}
   356	
   357	\begin{proof}
   358	  Write $Q_\sigma^E = I-\Pi_\sigma^E$. Split $D_\sigma$ into its growing and
   359	  complementary parts in~\eqref{E:compact-F-block} and use the two tail
   360	  integrals in the preceding proof. The exact $E$ component of
   361	  $P_\sigma(t)Q_\sigma(e,c)$ is
   362	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-complement-forcing}
   363	    P_\sigma^E(t)Q_\sigma^Ee
   364	    +\int_0^tP_\sigma^E(t-r)Q_\sigma^ED_\sigma C(r)c\ud r
   365	    -e_\sigma^E\ell_\sigma^C(C(t)c),
   366	  \end{equation}
   367	  and the constant component is $C(t)c$. The final subtraction retains the
   368	  growing response to constants in the projection. Since $\|Q_\sigma^ED_\sigma
   369	  C(r)\| \le C(1+r)$, the integral in~\eqref{E:compact-complement-forcing} has
   370	  norm at most
   371	  \[
   372	    Ce^{\mu_\sigma t}|c|
   373	    \int_0^t(1+t-r)(1+r)\ud r
   374	    =Ce^{\mu_\sigma t}(t+t^2+t^3/6)|c|.
   375	  \]
   376	  The first term is bounded by $C(1+t)e^{\mu_\sigma t}\|e\|_E$; the final term
   377	  and constant component by $C(1+t)|c|$. Since $\mu_\sigma \ge 0$ this proves
   378	  \eqref{E:compact-F-complement}. The boundedness of $(1+t)^3e^{-(d_0-\eta)t}$
   379	  proves \eqref{E:compact-normalized-complement}. In particular, the
   380	  constant-velocity polynomial is included in this estimate.
   381	
   382	  Put $\mathcal{B}_\sigma = iB_F(V_\sigma)$ and $d_{\sigma,\tau} =
   383	  \|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_\infty+ \|V_\sigma-V_\tau\|_2$. The bound for $B_F$ gives
   384	  $\|\mathcal{B}_\sigma-\mathcal{B}_\tau\| \le d_{\sigma,\tau}$. Subtract the
   385	  two free-Duhamel equations on states. Their difference is the sum of the
   386	  integral with $S_F(t-r)\mathcal{B}_\sigma(P_\sigma(r)-P_\tau(r))$ and that
   387	  with $S_F(t-r)(\mathcal{B}_\sigma-\mathcal{B}_\tau)P_\tau(r)$. The uniform
   388	  finite-horizon bounds and scalar Gronwall prove
   389	  \eqref{E:compact-parameter-flow}. The operator norm is measurable:
   390	  separability of $F$ expresses it as the supremum over a countable dense set of
   391	  unit states, each with continuous image. Hence, Gronwall applies without a
   392	  $\mathcal{B}(F)$-valued derivative or operator-norm continuity of the free
   393	  group. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:compact-F-complement}.
   394	\end{proof}

   256	  $C_{\mathrm{gap}}e^{-\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}t}$. Define positive margins and
   257	  finite bounds

   259	    a_*=\inf_I\ell_s(e_0),\quad j_*=\inf_I O_\phi(e_s),\quad
   260	    M_e=\max(1,\sup_I\|e_s\|),\quad
   261	    M_\ell=\max(1,\sup_I\|\ell_s\|).
   262	  \]

   264	  \|e_0\| = 1$ and $H_{\mathrm{obs}} = \max(1,\|O_\phi\|)$. Choose the aperture

   277	    M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z&\le\vartheta/4,\\

     1	\section{The temporal equilibrium density}
     2	\label{S:temporal-equilibrium}
     3	
     4	The density in Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium} is the classical interval
     5	Riesz equilibrium density. Its probability-normalized form on $[-1,1]$ is
     6	recalled by Calef and Hardin~\cite{calef.hardin:source2008:riesz}*{p.~1}.
     7	We prove the potential identity with the normalization used here.
     8	
     9	We use Euler's function $\Gamma_E(x) = \int_0^\infty u^{x-1}e^{-u}\ud u$, $x >
    10	0$, and $\operatorname{Beta}(x,y) = \int_0^1t^{x-1}(1-t)^{y-1}\ud t$, $x,y > 0$.
    11	Both integrals are positive and finite.
    12	
    13	\begin{lemma}[Gamma and Beta identities]\label{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}
    14	  For positive arguments,
    15	  \begin{align*}
    16	    \Gamma_E(x+1)&=x\Gamma_E(x),\\
    17	    \operatorname{Beta}(x,y)
    18	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(y)}{\Gamma_E(x+y)},\\
    19	    \Gamma_E(2x)
    20	    &=\frac{2^{2x-1}\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(x+1/2)}{\sqrt\pi}.
    21	  \end{align*}
    22	\end{lemma}
    23	
    24	\begin{proof}
    25	  Integration by parts gives the recurrence, with vanishing boundary terms. In
    26	  the positive product Gamma integral, use $(u,v) = (Rt,R(1-t))$, with Jacobian
    27	  $R$; Tonelli gives the Beta--Gamma identity. For the last identity, symmetry,
    28	  then $t = (1+v)/2$ and $v^2 = w$, give $\operatorname{Beta}(x,x) =
    29	  2^{1-2x}\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,x)$. Also $\Gamma_E(1/2) = \int_\R e^{-z^2}\ud
    30	  z = \sqrt\pi$: the substitution $u = z^2$ gives the first equality, and
    31	  squaring the positive Gaussian integral and using polar coordinates gives
    32	  $2\pi\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2}\ud r = \pi$. Substituting these into the
    33	  Beta--Gamma identity proves duplication. This proves
    34	  Lemma~\ref{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}.
    35	\end{proof}
    36	
    37	\begin{lemma}[Exact potential and mass]\label{L:temporal-equilibrium}
    38	  For $0 < a < 1$ put $r = (1-a)/2$ and, for $0 < t < 1$,
    39	  \begin{equation}\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-density}
    40	    f_a(t)=\frac{[t(1-t)]^{-r}}{\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}.
    41	  \end{equation}
    42	  This positive function belongs to $L^1(0,1)\cap L^2(0,1)$, and
    43	  \begin{align}
    44	    \int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_a(t)\ud t&=1
    45	    &&\text{for every }s\in[0,1],\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}\\
    46	    M_a:=\int_0^1f_a(t)\ud t
    47	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E((1+a)/2)}
    48	    {\Gamma_E(1+a)\Gamma_E((1-a)/2)}>0.
    49	    \label{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}
    50	  \end{align}
    51	\end{lemma}
    52	
    53	\begin{proof}
    54	  The positive binomial series $(1-z)^{-p} = \sum_{n\ge0}(p)_nz^n/n!$, $p > 0$,
    55	  $0 \le z < 1$, follows directly as follows. Its coefficient ratio gives
    56	  uniform convergence on compact subintervals, including for its derivative.
    57	  Termwise differentiation gives $(1-z)y' = py$, $y(0) = 1$; hence $(1-z)^py$ is
    58	  constant one. Here $(p)_0 = 1$, $(p)_n = p(p+1)\cdots(p+n-1)$. All terms used
    59	  below are nonnegative, so Tonelli applies.
    60	
    61	  For $0 < s < 1$ split the integral of $|s-t|^{2r-1}[t(1-t)]^{-r}$ into left
    62	  and right parts. In the left part, $t = su$ gives
    63	  \begin{align*}
    64	    L(s)
    65	    &=s^r\int_0^1(1-u)^{2r-1}u^{-r}(1-su)^{-r}\ud u\\
    66	    &=\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)s^r
    67	    \sum_{n\ge0}
    68	    \frac{(r)_n(1-r)_ns^n}{(1+r)_n n!}.
    69	  \end{align*}
    70	  The Beta ratio follows from the Gamma recurrence. Since $(r)_n/(1+r)_n =
    71	  r/(r+n)$, expanding the incomplete Beta integral gives
    72	  \[
    73	    L(s)=r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)B_s(r,r),\qquad
    74	    B_s(r,r)=\int_0^s u^{r-1}(1-u)^{r-1}\ud u.
    75	  \]
    76	  Reflection makes the right part $L(1-s)$, while symmetry gives
    77	  $B_s(r,r)+B_{1-s}(r,r) = \operatorname{Beta}(r,r)$. The full integral is
    78	  therefore $r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)\operatorname{Beta}(r,r) =
    79	  \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$. All integrals are finite because $-r > -1$ and
    80	  $2r-1 > -1$. At $s = 0$ the integral is directly $\operatorname{Beta}(r,1-r) =
    81	  \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$; $s = 1$ follows by reflection. This proves
    82	  \eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}, including the endpoints without a
    83	  limiting argument there.
    84	
    85	  Integrability and square integrability follow from $-r > -1$ and $-2r = a-1 >
    86	  -1$. Finally,
    87	  \[
    88	    M_a=
    89	    \frac{\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,1-r)}
    90	    {\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}
    91	    =\frac{\Gamma_E(1-r)}{\Gamma_E(2-2r)\Gamma_E(r)},
    92	  \]
    93	  which is~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}. Its time mass has not been
    94	  renormalized. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium}.
    95	\end{proof}
     1	\section{Physical spatial pairings and the full occupation class}
     2	\label{S:spatial-occupation-foundation}
     3	
     4	Retain a nonzero original covariance from Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} with its
     5	amplitude. Set $a = \alpha_0$, $k = 3-\alpha > 1$, $q = 4-\alpha = k+1$ and $D =
     6	q-2a > 0$. The scalar $D$ is fixed. All profiles are real. The original positive
     7	temporal exponent and threshold imply $\alpha < 2$; this is the strict
     8	inequality used in the scalar powers and concavity. The finite variational value
     9	over nonnegative controls $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$ is that of
    10	Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores}.
    11	
    12	\begin{lemma}[The physical two-point integral]\label{L:spatial-physical-pair}
    13	  The positive measure $\nu(\ud x,\ud y) = \ud x\,\Gamma(\ud y)$ is
    14	  sigma-finite. For nonnegative functions define
    15	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-physical-pair}
    16	    B_\Gamma(f,h)=\int f(x)h(x-y)\nu(\ud x,\ud y)
    17	  \end{equation}
    18	  initially as an extended nonnegative integral, using finite Borel
    19	  representatives of Lebesgue classes. Its value is representative independent.
    20	  Lebesgue-a.e. convergence transfers to $\nu$-a.e. convergence at both
    21	  positions $x$ and $x-y$.
    22	\end{lemma}
    23	
    24	\begin{proof}
    25	  Local finiteness of $\Gamma$ gives sigma-finiteness on exhausting balls, and
    26	  Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite. If $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue null, Tonelli
    27	  applied first in $x$ gives $\nu\{x\in N\} = 0$ and $\nu\{x-y\in N\} = 0$,
    28	  because every fixed translate of $N$ is null. An arbitrary Lebesgue null set
    29	  has a Borel null superset. Thus, arbitrary versions are measurable in the
    30	  $\nu$ completion with the same value, and the same observation applies to the
    31	  exceptional sets of a.e. convergence. Signed pairings will be used only after
    32	  absolute convergence. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-physical-pair}.
    33	\end{proof}
    34	
    35	Put $A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g) = B_\Gamma(g^2,g^2)$ and $b(g) = \|\nabla g\|_2^2$ on
    36	$H^1$; initially $A_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is used only for smooth compact profiles
    37	before the extension below. For smooth compact $z$, write $U_z = \Gamma*z$ in
    38	its usual pointwise sense.
    39	
    40	\begin{lemma}[Smooth temporal controls]\label{L:spatial-static-controls}
    41	  For every nonnegative nonzero $z \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$, let
    42	  \[
    43	    \lambda_z(c)^2=
    44	    \sup_{\substack{g\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|g\|_2=1}}
    45	    \left(c\int U_zg^2-b(g)\right),\qquad c>0.
    46	  \]
    47	  This is positive and finite, and $\lambda_z$ is Lipschitz on every compact
    48	  positive $c$ interval. With the exact $M_a$
    49	  in~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass},
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-static-score}
    51	    S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}\ge
    52	    \lambda_z(1)-\frac{M_a}{2}B_\Gamma(z,z).
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{lemma}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  Choose nonnegative nonzero $f \in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ and $s_0 = 1/2$. Let
    58	  $k_f(s_0) = \int_0^1|s_0-t|^{-a}f(t)\ud t > 0$. The smooth test $\Psi(t,x) =
    59	  cf(t)z(x)/k_f(s_0)$ has mean $cU_z$ at $s_0$.
    60	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-unmasked-rate} gives boundedness of this
    61	  potential, the displayed real Rayleigh formula, and a positive rate for every
    62	  $c > 0$. Comparing identical unit tests makes $\lambda_z(c)^2$ Lipschitz with
    63	  constant $\|U_z\|_\infty$. On a positive compact interval its rate has a
    64	  positive floor by monotonicity, giving the square-root Lipschitz bound.
    65	
    66	  Use the nonincreasing smooth cutoff $\chi$ constructed in the proof of
    67	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-remove-mask}. For integers $n \ge 4$, set on
    68	  $(0,1)$
    69	  \[
    70	    f_n(t)=f_a(t)\chi(1/(nt))\chi(1/(n(1-t))),\qquad
    71	    k_n(s)=\int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_n(t)\ud t.
    72	  \]
    73	  Extend $f_n$ by zero. It is smooth compact, vanishes near both endpoints, is
    74	  nonzero, and increases to $f_a$. Thus, $\Psi_n = f_n\otimes z$ is a positive
    75	  smooth control. Monotone convergence
    76	  and~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential} give $k_n(s)\uparrow1$ for every
    77	  $s \in [0,1]$. Since the kernel is at least one on the unit square off its
    78	  null diagonal, $0 < c_0: = \int_0^1f_4 \le k_n(s) \le 1$. The mean is
    79	  $k_n(s)U_z$; hence its rate is $\lambda_z(k_n(s))$, converging to
    80	  $\lambda_z(1)$ and bounded by that finite number. Dominated convergence gives
    81	  $I_{\Psi_n} \to \lambda_z(1)$.
    82	
    83	  The Gaussian cost is exactly the nonnegative Tonelli pairing
    84	  \[
    85	    v_{\Psi_n}=B_\Gamma(z,z)\int_0^1f_n(s)k_n(s)\ud s.
    86	  \]
    87	  Its time integrand increases to $f_a$, so the cost tends to
    88	  $M_aB_\Gamma(z,z)$. The spatial factor is finite and positive: its smooth
    89	  compact autocorrelation is positive near zero, and homogeneity scales any
    90	  origin-centered ball of positive $\Gamma$ mass to every other positive radius.
    91	  Such a ball exists by exhaustion. Take the limit of the individual
    92	  inequalities $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}} \ge I_{\Psi_n}-v_{\Psi_n}/2$. The variational
    93	  expression differences need not increase. No control depends on original large
    94	  time and no rough stochastic evolution has been used. This proves
    95	  Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-static-controls}.
    96	\end{proof}
   101	\begin{lemma}[Deterministic Fourier bound for the spatial energy]
   102	  \label{L:spatial-fourier-bound}
   103	  Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, allowing $\Gamma=0$, let
   104	  $g\in C_c^\infty(\R^d;\R)$ satisfy $\|g\|_2=1$ and put
   105	  $b=\|\nabla g\|_2^2$. Then $b>0$ and
   106	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-fourier-bound}
   107	    0\le A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)
   108	    \le 2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2},
   109	  \end{equation}
   110	  where $R_\alpha$ is defined in~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}.
   111	\end{lemma}
   112	
   113	\begin{proof}
   114	  If $b=0$, smoothness makes $\nabla g=0$ everywhere. Thus, $g$ is constant,
   115	  and compact support forces $g=0$, contrary to $\|g\|_2=1$. Put $Q=g^2$ and
   116	  use the unnormalized Fourier transform
   117	  \[
   118	    \mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)=\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q(x)\ud x.
   119	  \]
   120	  In the unitary convention of Section~\ref{S:masked-covariance}, this is
   121	  $c_d^{-1}\widehat Q$, with $c_d=(2\pi)^{-d/2}$.
   122	  The autocorrelation
   123	  \[
   124	    c_Q(y)=\int_{\R^d}Q(x)Q(x-y)\ud x
   125	  \]
   126	  is smooth and compactly supported. Apply the distributional spectral
   127	  identity~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to this Schwartz function.
   128	  Its inner Fourier integral is $|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2$, since $Q$ is real.
   129	  Hence
   130	  \[
   131	    A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)=\int c_Q(y)\Gamma(\ud y)
   132	    =\int|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\mu(\ud\xi).
   133	  \]
   134	  Both integrals are finite: $c_Q$ is compactly supported and $\Gamma$ is
   135	  Radon, while $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|^2$ is Schwartz and $\mu$ is tempered.
   136	  No density of either measure is required.
   137	
   138	  Since $\|Q\|_1=1$, we have $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|\le1$. Integration by parts
   139	  and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality give
   140	  \[
   141	    |\xi|\,|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|
   142	    \le\|\nabla Q\|_1
   143	    \le2\|g\|_2\|\nabla g\|_2=2\sqrt b.
   144	  \]
   145	  Splitting into $|\xi|^2\le4b$ and $|\xi|^2>4b$ therefore yields
   146	  \[
   147	    |\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\le\frac{8b}{4b+|\xi|^2}.
   148	  \]
   149	  The deterministic resolvent calculation in the proof of
   150	  Lemma~\ref{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}, together
   151	  with~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}, gives, for $q>0$,
   152	  \[
   153	    \mathcal{R}_\Gamma(q):=\int\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{q^2+|\xi|^2}
   154	    =q^{\alpha-2}R_\alpha<\infty.
   155	  \]
   156	  Consequently,
   157	  \[
   158	    A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)\le8b\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(2\sqrt b)
   159	    =2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2}.
   160	  \]
   161	  Nonnegativity follows from the spectral identity. If $\Gamma=0$, then
   162	  $\mu=0$ and both sides of~\eqref{E:spatial-fourier-bound} vanish. This proves
   163	  Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-fourier-bound}.
   164	\end{proof}
